results.title: Iris: Climbing to the Search Frontier

groq.claim: Iris-mini (35B) and Iris-pro (397B) search agents achieve the strongest open‑source results on BrowseComp, BrowseComp‑ZH, DeepSearchQA, and HLE within their parameter ranges.
groq.evidence: With context management enabled the models reach 82.2/84.8/86.9/52.3 (Iris‑mini) and 88.6/85.1/92.9/56.4 (Iris‑pro), surpassing all reported open‑source agents on those benchmarks.

groq.claim: The training data are generated by reverse‑constructing multi‑hop question chains from a web‑page hyperlink graph and rewriting every non‑answer entity into a descriptive reference to prevent string‑matching shortcuts.
groq.evidence: The authors author multi‑hop chains over an entity graph distilled from a seed page and its out‑links, then rewrite each non‑answer entity into a descriptive reference before filtering trajectories for SFT.

groq.claim: Trajectory filtering is performed at both the trajectory and turn level before supervised fine‑tuning, ensuring only high‑quality examples are used for SFT.
groq.evidence: Questions are turned into trajectories, which are filtered at both the trajectory and the turn level before SFT.

groq.claim: Training alternates supervised fine‑tuning and reinforcement learning against live search in a procedure called SFT‑RL climbing, using an internal reward judge and observation summarizer and resuming over‑long rollouts from their committed prefix.
groq.evidence: The policy is optimized by RL against live search with the reward judge and observation summarizer served inside the training cluster, and over‑long rollouts are interrupted at the request level and resumed from their committed prefix; the two stages are alternated in SFT‑RL climbing.

groq.claim: Inference‑time context management—controlling tool usage and context limits—provides a larger performance boost than most reported system differences, as shown by evaluating each benchmark with and without it while keeping tool set, context limit, and judge fixed.
groq.evidence: Because inference‑time context management is worth more on these benchmarks than most reported differences, the authors evaluate every benchmark both with and without it, holding the tool set, context limit, and judge fixed.

qwen.claim: Reverse-constructing multi-hop search tasks from web hyperlink structures and filtering for questions that fail closed-book but succeed with evidence yields high-quality training data for search agents.
qwen.evidence: The authors describe a data pipeline where tasks are authored over entity graphs, non-answer entities are rewritten to prevent string matching, and only questions solvable with supporting evidence but not closed-book are admitted.

qwen.claim: Alternating Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) and Reinforcement Learning (RL) in a 'SFT-RL climbing' procedure, where the hardest and most efficient rollouts from RL are fed back into the next SFT pass, improves search agent performance.
qwen.evidence: The paper presents this alternating training recipe as the core method behind Iris-mini and Iris-pro, which achieve strong results on benchmarks like BrowseComp and DeepSearchQA.

qwen.claim: Inference-time context management provides a larger performance gain on search benchmarks than the differences typically reported between different search agent systems.
qwen.evidence: The authors assert that context management is worth more on these benchmarks than most reported system differences and evaluate all benchmarks with and without it to isolate this effect.

qwen.claim: A single ReAct agent without sub-agents or test-time verification can achieve state-of-the-art results among open-source search agents when combined with effective context management and SFT-RL training.
qwen.evidence: Iris-pro reaches 88.6 on BrowseComp and 92.9 on DeepSearchQA using a single ReAct agent, which the authors identify as the strongest overall results in its parameter range.

qwen.claim: Interrupting over-long rollouts at the request level and resuming them from their committed prefix in the next step is a viable strategy for RL training of search agents against live search.
qwen.evidence: The training recipe includes this specific mechanism for handling over-long rollouts during the RL phase, with the reward judge and observation summarizer served inside the training cluster.

results.title: MaxKernel: Agentic Kernel Generation for TPUs

groq.claim: MaxKernel’s multi‑agent system generates TPU kernels that match expert hand‑tuned baselines on the JaxBench suite and real‑world model workloads.
groq.evidence: Evaluation on 50 diverse JaxBench tasks and complex open‑source model kernels shows performance on par with expert‑crafted implementations.

groq.claim: The Graph‑Based Autonomous Search paradigm scales the fully autonomous agent to globally explore the kernel design space, yielding significant performance improvements across the benchmark.
groq.evidence: Benchmark results demonstrate that the graph‑based search variant consistently outperforms the baseline autonomous agent and approaches expert performance.

groq.claim: Integrating real‑time compiler feedback with LLM‑driven sub‑agents enables effective self‑debugging and iterative optimization of generated kernels.
groq.evidence: The system’s sub‑agents use compiler diagnostics during planning and testing phases, and the reported metrics show accelerated convergence to high‑performance kernels.

groq.claim: A shared pool of specialized sub‑agents (planning, implementation, self‑debugging, testing, profiling) supports both Human‑in‑the‑Loop and fully autonomous kernel generation paradigms.
groq.evidence: The paper describes three paradigms—HITL, Auto, and Graph‑Based Search—all reusing the same sub‑agent modules to accomplish kernel development tasks.

qwen.claim: A multi-agent system combining LLMs with real-time compiler feedback can generate TPU kernels that match expert hand-tuned baselines on diverse benchmark tasks.
qwen.evidence: The authors demonstrate that MaxKernel consistently generates highly optimized implementations matching expert hand-tuned baselines on JaxBench (50 diverse kernel tasks) and real-world workloads.

qwen.claim: Integrating a metric/trace-driven optimization loop within an autonomous agent enables automated performance tuning for accelerator kernels without human intervention.
qwen.evidence: The 'Autonomous (Auto)' agent paradigm executes a fully automated, metric/trace-driven optimization loop, contributing to the system's ability to deliver significant performance across the benchmark.

qwen.claim: Graph-based autonomous search can scale agent-based kernel optimization for global exploration of the hardware design space.
qwen.evidence: The 'Graph-Based Autonomous Search' paradigm is described as scaling the Auto agent for global exploration of the design space, part of the system evaluated on JaxBench.

qwen.claim: Specialized sub-agents for planning, implementation, self-debugging, testing, and hardware profiling can be shared across different agentic paradigms (HITL, Autonomous, Graph-Based) for kernel generation.
qwen.evidence: The paper states that all three paradigms leverage a shared pool of specialized sub-agents to handle these specific tasks.

results.title: τ^τ-Bench: An Environment for End-To-End, Realistic Agent Construction

groq.claim: τ^τ-bench provides an end‑to‑end benchmark that tasks a developer LLM agent with constructing a complete customer‑service agent from real‑world inputs such as business records, client requirements, a production API, a codebase, and serving‑cost/model limits
groq.evidence: The abstract describes τ^τ‑bench as a benchmark that makes agent construction the task, giving the developer agent the same starting point a real engagement provides

groq.claim: The strongest tested configuration, Claude Opus 5 under Claude Code, passes only 23.9% of evaluation simulations across 53 tasks in τ^τ‑bench
groq.evidence: The abstract reports that the strongest configuration passes just 23.9% of evaluation simulations

groq.claim: An expert‑authored reference solution achieves an 82.2% success rate on τ^τ‑bench
groq.evidence: The abstract states that an expert‑authored reference ceiling scores 82.2%

groq.claim: Coding agents on τ^τ‑bench commonly fail by issuing shallow queries instead of deep comprehension, communicating almost nothing to the client, experimenting too little with agent architecture and serving spend, and shipping the first design that runs
groq.evidence: The abstract lists these failures as mirroring ones human agent developers see

qwen.claim: Coding agents currently fail to construct production-ready customer-service agents from realistic business records and constraints, with the strongest configuration passing only 23.9% of evaluation simulations.
qwen.evidence: The paper reports that Claude Opus 5 under Claude Code, the strongest tested configuration, achieved a pass rate of 23.9% across 53 tasks in the τ^τ-bench, significantly lower than the 82.2% score of an expert-authored reference ceiling.

qwen.claim: Primary failure modes for coding agents building LLM agents include issuing shallow queries instead of deep record comprehension, minimal communication with the client, and insufficient experimentation with agent architecture and serving costs.
qwen.evidence: The authors assert that observed failures mirror those of human developers, specifically noting that models ship the first design that runs without adequate experimentation or client interaction.

qwen.claim: τ^τ-bench evaluates agent construction capabilities by requiring a developer agent to build a complete customer-service agent from business records, client requirements, and production APIs, scored against held-out simulated users.
qwen.evidence: The benchmark design provides a developer agent with real-world engagement constraints (records, APIs, cost limits) and scores the resulting agent by deploying it against held-out simulated users across four domains.

results.title: RISE: Recursive Improvement via Self-Extrapolating Policy Distillation

groq.claim: RISE creates a synthetic teacher by extrapolating the displacement between the current model checkpoint and a trailing anchor in parameter or logit space, converting sparse outcome rewards into dense token‑level targets without any external model or privileged conditioning.
groq.evidence: The authors describe RISE as constructing a synthetic teacher directly from the model's own RLVR trajectory and extrapolating the displacement to turn a sparse outcome‑induced parameter update into a dense token‑level target, with no external model required.

groq.claim: RISE integrates RLVR outcome rewards with on‑policy distillation in a complementary loop where the rewards ground the extrapolation and the extrapolated teacher refines token‑level decisions.
groq.evidence: The paper states that RISE combines RLVR and OPD in a complementary loop: outcome rewards ground the extrapolation toward correct reasoning, while the extrapolated teacher refines token‑level decisions.

groq.claim: Because the synthetic teacher is refreshed each iteration as the student improves, RISE implements a recursive improvement mechanism rather than a one‑shot compression step.
groq.evidence: The authors note that the teacher is refreshed every iteration as the student improves, making distillation a recursive improvement mechanism instead of a one‑shot compression step.

groq.claim: Across mathematical reasoning, multi‑domain STEM, code generation, and multi‑turn agentic benchmarks, RISE consistently outperforms RLVR‑only training and on‑policy self‑distillation.
groq.evidence: Experiments spanning those domains show RISE outperforms RLVR‑only training and on‑policy self‑distillation across all settings.

qwen.claim: Constructing a synthetic teacher by extrapolating the displacement between the current checkpoint and a trailing anchor in parameter or logit space converts sparse RLVR outcome rewards into dense token-level distillation targets.
qwen.evidence: The paper introduces RISE, which uses this extrapolation mechanism to generate dense supervision without external models or privileged conditioning, and reports that it outperforms RLVR-only training across mathematical reasoning, STEM, code, and agentic tasks.

qwen.claim: Recursive on-policy distillation, where the teacher is refreshed every iteration from the student's own trajectory, improves performance over one-shot compression or static teacher distillation in RLVR settings.
qwen.evidence: Experiments show that RISE, which updates the teacher as the student improves, outperforms standard on-policy self-distillation and RLVR-only baselines across multiple domains.

qwen.claim: Combining outcome-based RLVR rewards with dense token-level supervision from a self-extrapolated teacher yields better reasoning accuracy than using either method in isolation.
qwen.evidence: The authors report that RISE outperforms both RLVR-only training and on-policy self-distillation across mathematical reasoning, multi-domain STEM, code generation, and multi-turn agentic tasks.

results.title: Refuse without Refusal: A Structural Analysis of Safety-Tuning Responses for Reducing False Refusals in Language Models

groq.claim: Boilerplate refusal statements in safety‑tuning data impede accurate discrimination between harmful and benign queries, leading to false refusals.
groq.evidence: Experiments and analyses show that the presence of a fixed refusal component causes models to rely on superficial cues and increases false‑refusal rates.

groq.claim: Training solely on rationales (Rationale‑Only) reduces false refusals while preserving comparable overall safety performance.
groq.evidence: The authors’ experiments demonstrate that models fine‑tuned only on the explanatory rationale achieve lower false‑refusal rates with safety metrics similar to full safety‑tuned models.

groq.claim: Rationale‑Only benefits persist when the model is used in an in‑context learning (ICL) configuration.
groq.evidence: Results indicate that the reduction in false refusals observed with Rationale‑Only fine‑tuning also appears when the model is prompted with examples at inference time.

groq.claim: Rationale‑Only training is compatible with existing inference‑time mitigation methods.
groq.evidence: The paper reports that combining Rationale‑Only fine‑tuning with evaluated inference‑time mitigations does not degrade safety or helpfulness performance.

groq.claim: Precisely curated, fine‑grained safety supervision datasets are necessary for aligning agents that balance helpfulness and safety.
groq.evidence: The authors conclude that the observed improvements stem from fine‑grained supervision, highlighting the need for carefully constructed safety datasets.

qwen.claim: Training safety-tuning models solely on refusal rationales, rather than boilerplate refusal statements, reduces false refusals while maintaining comparable safety performance.
qwen.evidence: Experiments and analyses in the paper show that refusal statements induce reliance on superficial cues, whereas rationale-only training improves discrimination between harmful and benign queries.

qwen.claim: Boilerplate refusal statements in safety-tuning datasets impede accurate discrimination between harmful and benign queries by causing models to rely on superficial linguistic cues.
qwen.evidence: The authors' structural analysis demonstrates that the presence of boilerplate refusal text correlates with higher rates of false refusals on benign inputs containing risky language.

qwen.claim: The benefits of rationale-only safety training are compatible with and persist in in-context learning (ICL) configurations and evaluated inference-time mitigation methods.
qwen.evidence: The paper reports that rationale-only benefits appear in ICL settings and remain compatible with inference-time mitigation strategies.

qwen.claim: Decomposing safety-tuning responses into boilerplate refusal statements and rationales allows for the isolation of the component responsible for false refusals.
qwen.evidence: The paper proposes this decomposition as a method to analyze and mitigate false refusals, showing that removing the boilerplate component improves helpfulness without sacrificing safety.

results.title: Ask Before You Optimize: Dynamic Pre-Formulation Clarification for Interactive Optimization

groq.claim: The authors introduce OR‑Clarify, a benchmark for pre‑formulation clarification that supports both open‑ended and choice‑based interactions and measures slot recovery, stopping behavior, silent assumptions, and interaction cost.
groq.evidence: The paper describes OR‑Clarify as a benchmark that presents partial problem descriptions, withholds hidden slots, and evaluates agents on those four metrics.

groq.claim: The Interactive Optimization (InterOPT) framework identifies unresolved formulation‑critical gaps and uses them to decide whether to ask the next clarification question or to stop.
groq.evidence: The authors propose a two‑stage InterOPT system that first detects missing slots and then guides the next action (question or stop).

groq.claim: In choice‑based experiments, InterOPT substantially outperforms all baselines in exact slot recovery.
groq.evidence: Choice‑based results reported in the paper show InterOPT achieving higher exact slot recovery scores than every baseline method evaluated.

groq.claim: In the open‑ended setting, InterOPT remains competitive with strong prior methods.
groq.evidence: Open‑ended experiments demonstrate that InterOPT’s performance is comparable to the best existing approaches on the same benchmark.

groq.claim: OR‑Clarify reframes OR assistance as a selective completeness decision: clarify when needed, stop when ready, and quantify what remains missing.
groq.evidence: The benchmark’s design and evaluation metrics are explicitly framed around deciding when to ask for clarification versus when to stop, quantifying remaining missing information.

qwen.claim: A two-stage framework that identifies unresolved formulation-critical gaps to guide clarification decisions outperforms baselines in exact slot recovery for interactive optimization tasks.
qwen.evidence: In choice-based experiments on the OR-Clarify benchmark, the proposed InterOPT framework substantially outperforms all baselines in exact slot recovery.

qwen.claim: Evaluations of LLMs for optimization modeling that assume complete problem specifications fail to capture the agent's ability to determine when clarification is necessary before formulation.
qwen.evidence: The authors assert that existing evaluations largely assume complete specifications, overlooking whether an agent knows when clarification is needed, which motivates the introduction of the OR-Clarify benchmark.

qwen.claim: OR-Clarify is a benchmark that evaluates agents on pre-formulation clarification by presenting partial problem descriptions with hidden slots and measuring slot recovery, stopping behavior, and interaction cost.
qwen.evidence: The paper introduces OR-Clarify, which supports open-ended and choice-based clarification and measures specific metrics including slot recovery and silent assumptions.

results.title: Don't Drop Dropout: Optimizing Layer Sparsity for Efficient LLM Training and Inference

groq.claim: Optimally configured layer dropout reduces training loss for the same number of FLOPs compared to training without layer dropout.
groq.evidence: The authors report that with optimal layer distribution, time schedule, and optimizer hyperparameters, layer dropout leads to lower loss at equal training FLOPs across many experiments.

groq.claim: Layer dropout enables up to 25% reduction in training FLOPs while achieving comparable or lower validation loss for a fixed number of training steps.
groq.evidence: Experiments show that for a given number of training steps, models using layer dropout save up to 25% of training FLOPs and attain lower or similar validation loss.

groq.claim: Layer dropout facilitates post‑training optimizations such as early exit, intermediate‑layer skipping, and self‑speculative decoding, delivering up to 1.5× inference speedup with negligible accuracy loss.
groq.evidence: The study demonstrates that these post‑training techniques, enabled by layer dropout, achieve up to 1.5× faster inference while maintaining accuracy.

groq.claim: The benefits of layer dropout generalize across model sizes from 271 M to 8.2 B parameters and datasets up to 160 B tokens.
groq.evidence: Across more than 2400 training experiments spanning the stated model and dataset scales, the reported gains consistently appear.

groq.claim: Layer dropout should be incorporated into state‑of‑the‑art LLM pre‑training recipes as a best practice.
groq.evidence: The authors conclude that layer dropout, when properly tuned, yields training and inference advantages and thus ought to be used in modern LLM training pipelines.

qwen.claim: Optimizing layer dropout hyperparameters (distribution, schedule, optimizer) results in lower training loss at the same FLOPs budget for large language models.
qwen.evidence: The authors report that with optimal settings, layer dropout leads to lower loss compared to no dropout when training FLOPs are held constant, based on over 2,400 experiments ranging from 271M to 8.2B parameters.

qwen.claim: Layer dropout allows LLMs to achieve lower or similar validation loss while saving up to 25% of training FLOPs for a fixed number of training steps.
qwen.evidence: Experimental results across models up to 8.2B parameters demonstrate that layer dropout reduces the computational cost of training by up to 25% without degrading validation loss.

qwen.claim: Layer dropout enables post-training inference optimizations such as early exit, intermediate-layer skipping, and self-speculative decoding, yielding up to 1.5x inference speedup with negligible accuracy loss.
qwen.evidence: The study demonstrates that models trained with layer dropout support these specific inference-time pruning and decoding strategies, achieving significant speedups without substantial performance degradation.

results.title: WorldReward: Reward Modeling for Camera-Conditioned World Models

groq.claim: WorldReward is a vision‑language‑model based pairwise preference reward that jointly evaluates action consistency and visual quality for camera‑conditioned world models.
groq.evidence: The abstract describes WorldReward as a VLM‑based pairwise preference reward model that unifies action‑consistency and visual‑quality evaluation for camera‑conditioned world models.

groq.claim: WorldReward splits paired videos into action‑aligned chunks, structures visual evidence for each chunk, and aggregates chunk‑level decisions by voting to produce separate video‑level action and visual‑quality preferences.
groq.evidence: The abstract states that WorldReward decomposes paired videos into action‑aligned chunks, organizes each chunk into structured visual evidence, and aggregates chunk‑level decisions by voting into video‑level preferences.

groq.claim: The authors built a large‑scale reasoning‑augmented preference dataset using judgments generated by a frontier VLM, refined through tool‑based agent auditing and targeted human review.
groq.evidence: The abstract notes that a large‑scale reasoning‑augmented preference dataset is constructed using structured judgments generated by a frontier VLM and refined via tool‑based agent auditing and human review.

groq.claim: WorldReward attains the highest agreement with human preferences on action consistency, appearance quality, and motion quality, outperforming GPT‑5.5 by 3.42, 1.45, and 3.56 percentage points respectively.
groq.evidence: WorldReward‑Bench results show WorldReward exceeds GPT‑5.5 by 3.42, 1.45, and 3.56 pp on the three dimensions, achieving the highest human‑agreement scores.

groq.claim: When used as the reward in RL post‑training of HY‑WorldPlay 1.5, WorldReward consistently improves both action execution and visual quality across short‑ to long‑term horizons.
groq.evidence: The abstract reports that using WorldReward for RL post‑training of HY‑WorldPlay 1.5 consistently improves action execution and visual quality over various horizons.

qwen.claim: Decomposing paired videos into action-aligned chunks and aggregating chunk-level VLM decisions via voting improves reward model agreement with human preferences over evaluating complete long videos against full action sequences.
qwen.evidence: The authors posit that full-context evaluation dilutes short-lived local action evidence; WorldReward achieves the highest agreement on action consistency, appearance, and motion quality on WorldReward-Bench, exceeding GPT-5.5 by 3.42, 1.45, and 3.56 percentage points respectively.

qwen.claim: A VLM-based pairwise preference reward model that unifies action-consistency and visual-quality evaluation can be used for RL post-training to improve both action execution and visual quality in camera-conditioned world models.
qwen.evidence: When used for RL post-training of HY-WorldPlay 1.5, WorldReward consistently improves both action execution and visual quality across short- to long-term horizons.

qwen.claim: Constructing a preference dataset using structured judgments from a frontier VLM, refined through tool-based agent auditing and targeted human review, yields a reward model that outperforms direct VLM evaluation on world model benchmarks.
qwen.evidence: WorldReward, trained on this reasoning-augmented dataset, exceeds GPT-5.5 by up to 3.56 percentage points in agreement with human preferences on WorldReward-Bench.
